headings.title: Introduction to Carbohydrates in Maternal Nutrition
headings.content: Carbohydrates serve as the primary source of dietary energy for pregnant and lactating women. During pregnancy, maternal metabolism shifts significantly to ensure a steady supply of glucose—the preferred fuel for the developing feto-placental unit. As the pregnancy advances, the body naturally develops a degree of insulin resistance. This ingenious metabolic adaptation preserves circulating glucose for the growing fetus rather than letting maternal tissues consume it all. Midwives must understand that cutting out carbohydrates entirely during pregnancy deprives both mother and baby of essential fuel. Instead of restriction, the focus should remain on consuming quality, nutrient-dense carbohydrate foods that also supply vital vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

headings.title: Chemical Classification and Types of Carbohydrates
headings.content:
Dietary carbohydrates are chemically grouped based on their molecular structure into simple and complex forms.

- **Monosaccharides**: Single-unit sugars like glucose, fructose, and galactose that require no digestion before absorption.
- **Disaccharides**: Two sugar units bonded together, including sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), and maltose.
- **Polysaccharides**: Long, complex chains of glucose molecules found in starches and dietary fiber, which take longer to break down.

Simple sugars cause rapid spikes in blood glucose, whereas complex carbohydrates digest slowly, providing sustained energy and supporting regular bowel movements through fiber content.

headings.title: Dietary Sources for Pregnant and Lactating Women
headings.content:
In the Nigerian context, mothers have access to an abundance of rich, wholesome carbohydrate staples. Advising pregnant women requires focusing on local foods that offer maximum nutritional value.

- **Whole Grains**: Brown rice, local Ofada rice, sorghum (guinea corn), millet, and whole maize.
- **Tubers and Roots**: Yam, cassava products like garri and fufu, and sweet potatoes, preferably eaten with fiber-rich soups.
- **Legumes and Fruits**: Beans, bambara nuts, plantains, bananas, and oranges, which provide both carbohydrates and vital micronutrients.

Refined flours and sugary drinks should be minimized because they offer empty calories without the protective fiber and B-vitamins found in unrefined options.

headings.title: Metabolic Functions and Fiber in Pregnancy
headings.content: Beyond simple energy production, carbohydrates perform critical biological roles during gestation. Glucose is mandatory for proper brain development in the fetus. Additionally, non-digestible carbohydrates—known as dietary fiber—play a starring role in maternal digestive health. Pregnancy hormones like progesterone slow down gut motility, frequently causing uncomfortable constipation and hemorrhoids. High-fiber foods add bulk to the stool and stimulate peristalsis, keeping the bowels moving smoothly. Furthermore, fermentable fibers nourish beneficial gut bacteria, supporting the overall immune health of both mother and baby.

headings.title: Clinical Significance and Common Disorders
headings.content: Imbalances in carbohydrate metabolism can lead to significant clinical complications in obstetric practice. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) occurs when the mother's pancreas cannot produce enough insulin to overcome pregnancy-related insulin resistance, leading to high blood sugar levels. This condition increases the risk of macrosomia, birth injuries, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Conversely, inadequate carbohydrate intake forces the body to break down fats for energy, producing ketone bodies that can cross the placenta and potentially harm fetal neurological development. Midwives play a front-line role in screening, patient education, and dietary counseling to prevent these extremes.
